# AGENTS.md

Rules for agents working in this repository. Each id names a statement in the stmt store, the source of truth; read one with `stmt get ID`.

## agentic

- Every write made with an API token first asks the stmt gate in the channel's scope (operations such as editorial.write); BLOCK or INDETERMINATE refuses it with 403, and a successful write emits its AFTER event, so stmt rules decide and record what agents may do. (`agentic.gate`)
- Every POST that creates something accepts an Idempotency-Key header, except token creation: its secret is shown once and never stored, so a lost response means revoking that token and creating another. A repeat with the same key and body returns the stored response with Idempotent-Replayed: true; the same key with a different body is refused with 422, and a key whose first request is still running with 409. Keys expire after 24 hours. (`agentic.idempotency`)
- Agents authenticate with personal API tokens: prefixed `sre_`, stored only as hashes, expiring (default 90 days, at most 365), revocable, limited to explicit scopes and, optionally, to some of the user's channels; other channels answer 404 and a limited token cannot create one. A token never grants more than its user's role, and only a signed-in session can create, list or revoke tokens. (`agentic.tokens.scoped`)
- Writes made with an API token record the token as author (stmt owner type `token`, id = token id); the token record names its user. (`agentic.audit`)
- Replaceable resources return an ETag. PUT, PATCH and DELETE on them accept If-Match and answer 412 when the resource changed, so an agent never overwrites a change it has not seen. (`agentic.concurrency.etag`)
- Every JSON error is an RFC 9457 problem (application/problem+json) with type, title, status, detail and instance. `detail` stays the human-readable English message; validation errors add an `errors` list naming each field. (`agentic.errors.problem`)
- An MCP server at /mcp exposes the main operations as tools. Tools call the service layer, never HTTP routes or SQL, authenticate with the same API tokens and enforce the same roles and scopes. (`agentic.mcp`)
- MCP clients such as claude.ai connect with OAuth 2.1 as the MCP authorization spec describes: the 401 from /mcp points to protected-resource metadata, and the app is its own authorization server with dynamic client registration, authorization code with PKCE (S256) and a consent page where the signed-in person picks the scopes. Approving issues an ordinary sre_ API token named after the client, so roles, scopes, expiry, revocation, the gate, audit and rate limits apply unchanged. (`agentic.oauth`)
- The OAuth endpoints (/.well-known metadata, /oauth/register, /oauth/token) follow the OAuth RFCs, not the API conventions: errors are {error, error_description} (RFC 6749) and registration takes no Idempotency-Key. Redirect URIs must be https or loopback http and match exactly, but a loopback one may use any port (RFC 8252 7.3), as native clients like Claude Code need. Codes are single-use, expire in 10 minutes and are stored only as hashes. (`agentic.oauth.protocol`)
- Every API operation has a stable snake_case operationId, a summary and a description written for an agent choosing which call to make. (`agentic.openapi.described`)
- List endpoints are paginated: `limit` (default 50, at most 200) and an opaque `cursor`; responses are {items, next_cursor}. (`agentic.pagination`)
- Each API token may make at most SREDITOR_AGENT_REQUESTS_PER_MINUTE requests a minute (default 120), counted together across the API and /mcp; signed-in sessions are not counted. Every 429 response carries a Retry-After header: the whole seconds until a request is allowed again. (`agentic.rate-limits`)
- Every MCP tool has a human title and declares all four annotations explicitly: readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint and openWorldHint (false, since tools act only inside sreditor). An undeclared hint defaults to the worst case, so a tool that only creates or edits would otherwise reach clients as destructive. (`agentic.mcp.annotations`)
- The MCP instructions name only tools the server registers, which a test checks, and every caller sees the same tool list. A call whose token lacks a scope or role returns a tool error naming what is missing and how to get it: a new token or connection with that scope, or a role from a channel owner, so an agent can tell an old deployment from a missing permission. (`agentic.mcp.discovery`)
- An MCP tool that fails returns a tool error (isError) the agent can act on: what went wrong, the field or value at fault and the call that fixes it, such as the tool that lists valid ids. Protocol errors are only for malformed requests. (`agentic.mcp.errors`)
- MCP moves files through short-lived signed links, since an agent's code cannot use the connection's token: get_file_link returns a single-use https URL valid 15 minutes for one brand file, media file, third-party copy or srstudio export; create_upload_link returns one that accepts one upload of one media kind into one episode, checked like the API upload. Files up to 1 MB, such as a logo, may come inline as base64. Links never open waivers; issuing one needs the role and scope of the API call it stands for. (`agentic.mcp.files`)
- Every MCP tool that creates something, uploads or spends credits takes an optional idempotency_key with the API's rules (agentic.idempotency): a repeat with the same key and arguments returns the first result marked replayed, different arguments are refused and keys expire after 24 hours, so an agent can retry after a timeout or a 502 without writing twice. (`agentic.mcp.idempotency`)
- A renamed MCP tool keeps answering under its old name for 90 days as an alias with the same arguments, whose description names the new tool and the date the alias ends; the instructions mention only the new name. (`agentic.mcp.renames`)
- MCP tools return structured content that matches a declared output schema, and list tools page with the same limit and cursor as the API (agentic.pagination), so no result floods the agent's context. (`agentic.mcp.results`)
- Follow the current MCP specification (2026-07-28): /mcp is stateless Streamable HTTP with JSON responses and keeps no session between requests, so any instance can answer any call. New code adopts none of the deprecated features: Roots, Sampling, Logging, the HTTP+SSE transport and, for clients that can use CIMD, dynamic client registration. (`agentic.mcp.spec`)
- MCP tool names, descriptions and schemas are fixed in code and never built from stored data, so text that people write, such as research notes, sources or screenplays, can never change what an agent is told a tool does. (`agentic.mcp.static-descriptions`)
- Design MCP tools around tasks an agent finishes in one or two calls, not one tool per HTTP route, and keep the set small. A tool's description says when to use it, when not to and what must exist first, for an agent choosing between tools. (`agentic.mcp.tools.outcomes`)
- The authorization server accepts Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) and advertises client_id_metadata_document_supported and authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported. It fetches an https client_id URL with SSRF protection (public addresses only; size and time limits), checks the client_id matches the URL and lists the redirect URI, and caches it as HTTP allows. A document listing none among its supported auth methods is a public PKCE client, like ChatGPT's. Registration stays for older clients. (`agentic.oauth.cimd`)
- Agents render through MCP: request_render queues a job and answers at once with its id, status and place in the queue, or a tool error listing what the episode still lacks; get_render reports status, progress and report findings and, when done, the video's media file and download link. A video never travels in a tool result: the agent downloads it through the API with the same token, or a person opens the link signed in. (`agentic.render.mcp`)
- Requesting or canceling a render needs the owner or editor role and, for a token, the render:write scope, and first asks the stmt gate for render.request, so stmt rules can cap how much a channel renders; reading a render needs channels:read. Worker tokens are not user tokens: they can only claim, report and upload jobs. (`agentic.render.scope`)

## agents

- Run subagents on Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5). (`agents.subagent.model`)

## deployment

- Deploy on Docker: ship every service as a Docker image. (`deploy.docker`)
- The development deployment is published at https://sreditor-dev.arc4d3.com through the Cloudflare tunnel sreditor-development (zone arc4d3.com); SREDITOR_PUBLIC_URL must match it, and `sreditor doctor` checks that it answers. Production subdomains stay one level deep (name.arc4d3.com), because the free certificate covers only *.arc4d3.com. (`deploy.dev.url`)
- Observe the app with Prometheus, Loki and Grafana in compose.yaml under the observability profile: the app serves request metrics labelled by route template on SREDITOR_METRICS_PORT, a port the tunnel never routes to; Grafana Alloy ships container logs to Loki; Grafana provisions both sources and the dashboards in deploy/observability, and only Grafana publishes a port, on loopback, behind a login. (`deploy.observability`)

## documentation

- Generate every document from the stmt store, the single source of truth. Never edit a generated document by hand: revise the statement and regenerate. (`docs.generated.from.stmt`)

## engineering

- Build HTTP APIs with FastAPI. (`code.api.fastapi`)
- Write all code and schemas in English, including identifiers, comments, and table, column and field names. (`code.language.english`)
- Define data models and schemas with Pydantic models. (`code.models.pydantic`)
- Keep test coverage above 90%. (`code.tests.coverage`)
- Never hard-code paths, URLs or secrets: read them from settings ([tool.sreditor] in pyproject.toml or environment variables via Pydantic settings). (`code.config.no-hardcoded`)
- Never use a bare except or swallow an exception silently: catch specific exceptions and either handle them or re-raise with context. (`code.errors.explicit`)
- Format and lint all Python with Ruff; CI fails on any ruff format or ruff check violation. (`code.style.ruff`)
- Type-annotate every function signature; the code must pass a strict type check (mypy --strict). (`code.types.strict`)
- Keep the relational schema in Boyce-Codd normal form: a column never repeats what another table already holds, unless a constraint keeps both in step. A row that links two items of a channel names the channel in each foreign key, so the database refuses a link across channels; JSON columns hold only a part stored and revised on its own (project.episodes). (`code.data.normalized`)
- Commit no dead code: no commented-out code, unused imports or unreachable branches. (`code.dead.none`)
- Give a function at most 5 parameters; group related parameters into a Pydantic model. (`code.functions.args`)
- Keep functions short and single-purpose: cyclomatic complexity at most 10 and about 40 lines at most. (`code.functions.small`)
- Keep layers separate: API routes hold no SQL or business logic and call the store/repository layer, which never imports FastAPI. (`code.layers.separation`)
- Name things for what they are or do: no abbreviations or single-letter names outside comprehensions, and booleans read as predicates (is_, has_). (`code.naming.intent`)
- Write comments that explain why, not what; give every public module, class and function a one-line docstring. (`code.comments.why`)
- Prefer frozen Pydantic models and pure functions; keep side effects such as database and filesystem access at the edges. (`code.immutability`)
- Use no magic numbers or strings: name them as module constants or enums. (`code.magic.none`)
- Make each test check one behaviour and name it after that behaviour: test_<unit>_<condition>_<expected>. Exception: a flow test follows one user journey across several pages (registration, password reset, invitation, sign in and out, and the e2e tests) and may check each step in order; name it after the journey and its outcome. (`code.tests.naming`)

## i18n

- Mark every user-facing string for translation (_() in templates, N_() in Python) and keep its pt-BR entry in src/sreditor/locales/pt-BR.json; tests fail when a marked string has no translation or a translation has no marked string. (`i18n.catalog`)
- Write every user-facing text in English, the base language, and translate it into Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR), the alternate language; English is the fallback for any missing translation. (`i18n.languages`)
- Keep the JSON API's error details and field names in English; only text meant for people (pages and emails) is translated. (`i18n.api.english`)
- Choose the language from the ?lang= switch, remembered in a cookie, then the Accept-Language header, then English; set <html lang> to it and send emails in the same language. (`i18n.negotiation`)
- Translate stmt prose shown to users, such as terms and privacy, in a sibling category suffixed with the lowercase locale (terms.pt-br); pages fall back to the English category when it is empty. (`i18n.prose`)

## project

- A social account (its platform and handle, ignoring a leading @ and letter case) belongs to at most one channel. A second channel claiming it is refused with 409 and told only that another channel holds it, never which, since channels stay private to their members. (`project.accounts.unique`)
- A channel's brand kit holds its identity as data: a display name people can change (the slug stays), colors as #RRGGBB with a role (primary, secondary, accent, text, background), fonts by role (heading, body, caption) with family, weight and an optional font file, logo, avatar and opening and closing stings. Owners and editors change it on pages, through the API and through MCP; a platform account may override any of it. (`project.brand`)
- An episode lists its claims: each figure or fact its screenplay or short script states, with the quote, where it appears and the sources, its own or its pitches', that back it, each marked primary or secondary and checked or not, with who checked and when. While a claim has no checked primary source the episode warns, without blocking any status, and the warning shows again when it moves to published. (`project.claims`)
- An episode keeps its editorial classification as a part of its own, in the closed vocabulary of Pedro's video-classification 1.0.0 taxonomy: audience, domains, purposes, genres, approaches, formats, visual techniques and styles, tones, emotional targets, creative and humor devices. Each dimension is present, absent, unknown or not applicable; a present one holds one primary and up to two secondary values. Values from an AI or mixed classification carry a confidence from 0 to 1. (`project.classification`)
- A classification whose genres include comedy names at least one humor device; a satirical approach names its target and the behaviour it criticises; a parodic approach names the work it parodies. An agent may propose a classification, but it stays a proposal, marked with its method, until a person reviews it. (`project.classification.checks`)
- A channel declares its profile in the same dimensions, and sreditor observes one from its classified episodes: for each value, how many episodes hold it as primary or secondary and its share of all classified episodes, unknown included. The profile page shows both side by side and warns when a declared primary value appears in fewer than half of the classified episodes. (`project.classification.profile`)
- Episodes, pitches and their sources, media files, third-party media and library entries each keep a context: short answers to what, who, where, when, why and how, stored and revised on its own. Any of them may link to another item of its channel under one of those questions, with a note, such as a pitch whose who is a character; each item lists its links and where it is mentioned. Removing an item removes its context and links. A person outside the library stays a name in the answer. (`project.context`)
- An episode keeps its delivery package, stored and revised on its own: per cut (such as main, vertical, teaser) the final video and cover as media files of the episode, caption, alt text and hashtags; per platform account the post link and publish time once posted. Moving to published warns, without blocking, when a cut lacks a video or a post lacks its link. (`project.delivery`)
- An episode belongs to one channel, is numbered within it and moves through the statuses idea, research, script, production and published. Its parts (editorial research, sources and waivers, screenplay, characters, locations, voice-over, sound, visual) are added one step at a time and each is stored and revised on its own, so editing one part never conflicts with another; characters, locations and visual style live in a channel library that episodes refer to. (`project.episodes`)
- Members download ready-made books of a pitch, an episode, the library, the channel or its rights and credits, picking sections, episodes by status or number range, and language: JSON (English field names, format version), Excel (one sheet per table) or a PDF with the channel's logo, colors and library pictures. Exports only read and never include waivers; only the srstudio zip carries audio. Excel cells are always text, never formulas; PDF rendering reads only the app's fonts and the channel's own files. (`project.export`)
- A channel's library holds third-party media made by others: videos, images, audio, documents, web pages, 3D models, textures and shaders, such as a NASA animation, a YouTube video it reacts to, a credited photo, a paper or a CC BY model. Each item keeps its link, creator, rights (public domain, open license, licensed, citation or fair use, own, unknown) with license and credit line, and may keep an uploaded copy under the episode media file rules. sreditor never downloads from the link. (`project.external-media`)
- A 3D model's copy is GLB, binary FBX or BLEND; a texture's PNG, JPEG, WebP, EXR, KTX2 or DDS; a shader's UTF-8 text without control bytes; any of the three may be a ZIP package, stored unopened and always downloaded. GLB and FBX copies show in a 3D viewer built on three.js vendored in static/vendor and loaded only on pages that show one; other files download. An episode may use such an item as a production element. (`project.external-media.3d`)
- An episode records each use of a third-party item on its own: the time range or pages, the purpose and the scene. An item in use cannot be removed until its episodes drop it. The episode lists the credits of what it uses and warns, without blocking any status, when rights are unknown, a citation or fair use gives no reason, or a required credit is missing. (`project.external-media.use`)
- An episode refers to its channel library by name: a character who speaks in its screenplay, or a place a scene heading names, matches the library entry with the same name ignoring case and spacing. A name with no entry is offered for adding and never added on its own, so typos do not fill the library. (`project.library.by-name`)
- An episode's media are files: voice-over, sound effects and score as audio (MP3, WAV or M4A), visual effects and renders as video (MP4 or WebM), covers as images (PNG, JPEG or WebP), each at most SREDITOR_MAX_MEDIA_BYTES (default 95 MB, under Cloudflare's 100 MB limit) except a render (project.render.upload). The type comes from the content, never the name; files go to disk in chunks, never whole into memory. Each has a name and a note people can change; the file never changes, so a new take is a new file. (`project.media`)
- A published post keeps dated snapshots of its numbers, entered on a page, the API or MCP and not fetched from platforms yet: views, reach, likes, comments, shares, saves, average watch time and retention per second, which may be imported from a platform's CSV. A channel compares its posts by these numbers, so pitches and hooks follow what worked on it. (`project.metrics`)
- A channel keeps pitches (pautas): story ideas with a title, a summary and a status (idea, research, approved, discarded), each with its own research notes and sources, stored and revised on their own. An episode may reference several pitches in order, the first its main one, and a pitch may feed several episodes; an episode shows each pitch's notes, sources and claims as they are, never a copy, next to its own research. A pitch that episodes reference cannot be deleted until they drop it. (`project.pitches`)
- sreditor is a social media channel manager and production tool: it manages channels, their accounts on each social platform, their brand kits and their Editorial guidelines, and produces their episodes, from research and screenplay to voice-over, sound and visuals. Build features in service of that purpose. (`project.purpose`)
- Owners and editors can render an episode into video. sreditor queues a job built from the episode's srstudio export at its current revisions and a preset; a render worker builds the scene with srstudio and encodes it with scene-render. The same export, preset and engine version reuses the earlier video and spends no GPU time. The finished video becomes a media file of the episode (kind render) with its scene-render report. (`project.render`)
- A render job moves through queued, building, rendering, encoding and then done, failed or canceled, and keeps its progress, its worker and the findings of its scene-render report. A worker holds a job on a lease it renews while it works; a job whose lease lapses returns to the queue, and one that fails three times stays failed with the reason. A queued or running job can be canceled. (`project.render.jobs`)
- A worker uploads the finished video in parts of at most SREDITOR_MAX_MEDIA_BYTES, under Cloudflare's request limit, each with its SHA-256, and completes it with the SHA-256 of the whole file, at most SREDITOR_MAX_RENDER_BYTES. Parts go to disk as they arrive, never whole into memory; an upload left incomplete expires after 24 hours. Downloads are not split. (`project.render.upload`)
- Render workers are GPU machines running the sreditor worker image (srstudio plus a pinned scene-render engine), registered by an instance admin. Each has its own worker token, pulls jobs over HTTPS and never needs an inbound port, reports its GPUs and engine version, takes srstudio's GPU lock around every engine call and renders with scene-render encode --parallel auto. Splitting one video across machines waits for scene-render to split and join it. (`project.render.workers`)
- An episode may have a short script for vertical video, stored and revised on its own: its length, language and voice, then blocks in order, each running from start_s to end_s with a function (hook, development, turn, punch, cta), speech with voice markup and an optional expected reaction with intensity 1-5, plus on-screen texts of at most 90 characters that work without sound. Broken markup or times are refused; gaps, a hook past 3 s, a missing final punch or too many words only warn. (`project.short-script`)
- sreditor stays compatible with srstudio, Pedro's scene-render toolkit: owners and editors export an episode as a zip srstudio reads unchanged: the take timeline (timeline.json, contiguous takes in seconds with word timings), a WAV per take with its SHA-256, the channel bible (bible/cast.json, relationships.json) and the beats (assets/poses.json). sreditor writes them from a pinned copy of srstudio's vocabularies, never importing srstudio, and lists each missing piece instead of exporting a broken file. (`project.srstudio`)
- A short-script block may carry beats, each at a time inside the block for one character of the cast: eyes, mouth, arms and wear from srstudio's closed toon vocabularies and an optional prop event. Beats are at least 0.15 s apart and the first starts at 0; a value outside the vocabulary is refused, and an episode whose style has no beats keeps them without exporting them. (`project.srstudio.beats`)
- A library character is a srstudio bible entry: world, status (canon or placeholder), kind (person, animal, object, archetype), the rig that draws it (such as toon-dog), look, who they are, comic role (straight, instigator, victim, chaos, know-it-all), what never changes, open questions and voice. Each canon fact cites a published episode of the channel, how it shows (line, drawn, voice, seen) and a quote. Places keep slug, world and description; the library records relationships between pairs of characters. (`project.srstudio.bible`)
- A channel's library also holds props: a name, slug, description and the srstudio registry name that draws it (such as laptop or papers). Beats refer to props by slug. (`project.srstudio.props`)
- Episodes, characters, places, props and visual styles carry a slug in srstudio's form (lowercase words joined by hyphens), unique within the channel, proposed from the name and editable until the first export; an episode also keeps an integer seed, so a rebuild in srstudio draws the same frames. (`project.srstudio.slugs`)
- A voice belongs to a character, not to a script: an ElevenLabs premade voice id and name with stability, similarity boost and style (0 to 1) and speed (0.7 to 1.2). Each short-script block names who speaks, a character of the channel's library or the episode's narrator voice, and its voice markup tags use srstudio's audio-tag names, so an export turns them into srstudio's direction fields (tags, emphasis, pauses) with the line text clean. (`project.srstudio.voice`)
- Long texts people and agents write (research notes, pitch notes and summaries, context answers, editorial guidelines) are Markdown. Pages and PDF books show them formatted through one renderer: headings, emphasis, lists, quotes, code and http, https or mailto links, never raw HTML or images. Where a summary is cut short it shows as plain text. JSON and MCP keep the text as written, Excel cells stay plain text, and MCP tool descriptions say which fields take Markdown. (`project.text.markdown`)
- A library visual style has a name, slug, look description, srstudio style (cutout, ink, soft, cel, stick, toon, collage, saga or gloss, which fixes frame size and fps) and, as data: palette (#RRGGBB by role), fonts by role, cut rhythm (shortest and average shot in seconds), smallest text in px at frame height and safe zone (% per edge). The srstudio export carries them in style.json. Each episode picks at most one style of its channel; removing it leaves those episodes without one. (`project.visual-style`)
- Owners and editors can generate an episode's voice-over from its short script with ElevenLabs; the key lives only in SREDITOR_ELEVENLABS_API_KEY, and without it the feature is hidden. Each block is its own take in its speaker's voice, with word timings; the same text, voice, settings, model and language reuses the earlier take and spends no credits. Takes join into a voice_over media file ending in a short fade and silence; measured block starts can replace planned times. Tests never call ElevenLabs. (`project.voice-generation`)
- Speech carries voice direction inline: [tag] or [tag:value] at a point, [tag]...[/tag] over a span, from one vocabulary defined once in voice_markup.py with each tag's ElevenLabs rendering per model (v2: <break> up to 3 s; v3: audio tags). Camera, sound and edit cues stay in the script for editing and are never spoken. Unknown tags, wrong values and unclosed spans are refused. (`project.voice-markup`)
- Before generating a voice-over, a person or agent can see its cost: per block the characters to speak and whether a stored take is reused, then the total characters and credits for the model. Each take returns its words with start and end in seconds through the API and MCP, and keeps a license record: provider, voice id and name, model, the account's plan and when it was made. A channel's brand may name a default narrator voice, used when a script names none. (`project.voice.estimate`)
- An episode's waivers are the signed releases behind it (image, voice or location rights): a PDF, JPEG or PNG file of at most SREDITOR_MAX_MEDIA_BYTES with who signed, when and what it covers. They hold personal data, so only owners and editors see or change them; a token reads them only with the waivers:read scope and changes them only with editorial:write as well. Their files always download, never display inline. (`project.waivers`)

## repository

- Keep the repository ready to publish on GitHub: a README, a LICENSE file and a .gitignore, with no secrets or local build artifacts committed. (`repo.github.ready`)
- License the project under the MIT License. (`repo.license.mit`)

## ui

- Build every page from the shared design system: Jinja macros in templates/_ui.html plus their CSS (button, field, card, alert, tag and so on). Add a new component there before using it, and show every component, in each state, theme and language, on a /design page that only runs in development. (`ui.design-system`)
- Cover every public flow (register, verify, sign in/out, password reset, invitation, language switch) and the app journey (channel, account, brand files, editorial, episode, research with source and pitch, screenplay, cast, short script, voice-over, waiver, style, third-party media, export, classify, invite, token, delete the channel) with Playwright in a real browser against the Docker build. They run only when Pedro asks (SREDITOR_E2E=1 or the CI job run by hand), since they overload the machine. (`ui.e2e.playwright`)
- Define every color, spacing step, radius, font size, shadow, duration and easing curve once, as design tokens (CSS custom properties) in src/sreditor/web/static/tokens.css, with light and dark values; components use only tokens, never raw values. (`ui.tokens`)
- Make every e2e run save evidence: a Playwright screenshot of each step at mobile (390px) and desktop (1280px) widths, in light and dark themes and in English and pt-BR, plus a trace for each failure. Write it to a git-ignored folder and attach it to the pull request. (`ui.e2e.evidence`)
- Give every action visible feedback: hover, focus-visible, pressed, loading (a submit button shows it is working and cannot be pressed twice), success and error states. Never leave the user guessing whether something happened. (`ui.microinteractions`)
- Animate with the motion tokens only: short durations (100-300 ms) and gentle easing curves (ease-out to enter, ease-in to leave), animating transform and opacity rather than layout; turn non-essential motion off under prefers-reduced-motion. Exception: a loading indicator turns for as long as its request runs, at its own token (--duration-spin); it is essential feedback, so it keeps turning under prefers-reduced-motion. (`ui.motion`)
- Ship polished UI: consistent spacing on the token scale, aligned edges, WCAG AA contrast in both themes, visible keyboard focus, no layout shift while loading, and layouts that work from 360px wide upward. (`ui.polish`)

## voice

- Trate o usuário pelo nome: Pedro. (`voice.address-by-name`)
- Não traga informações sem contexto; sempre deixe claro de onde vêm as informações. (`voice.cite-sources`)
- Peça decisão ao Pedro só quando ela importa para ele: produto, custo, segurança, dados de usuários, algo difícil de desfazer ou que muda como ele usa o sistema. Em escolhas técnicas internas, siga sua recomendação, faça e conte o que foi feito. (`voice.decide-what-matters`)
- Explique o problema, as causas, as possíveis soluções e suas consequências, e aponte sua recomendação. (`voice.explain-then-recommend`)
- Liste as opções como A, B, …; a opção recomendada fica em negrito. (`voice.options-format`)
- Use linguagem simples, sem termos desnecessários ou complexos; o usuário é inteligente. (`voice.plain-language`)

## web

- Registration and password-reset pages show the same response whether or not the email has an account. (`web.auth.no-enumeration`)
- Every email that carries a token links to the matching page with the token in the fragment (#token=), which browsers never send to servers; the page copies it into its form and removes it from the address bar, and without JavaScript the person pastes the whole link into the form. Never ask a user to call an API endpoint by hand. (`web.email.links`)
- Protect every state-changing form with a CSRF token (double-submit cookie) and reject a POST whose Origin header does not match the public URL. (`web.forms.csrf`)
- Build the public, unauthenticated area as server-rendered pages in the FastAPI app, with Jinja2 templates and HTMX, served from the same origin and Docker image as the API; do not add a separate frontend service for it. (`web.public.server-rendered`)
- Serve pages with a self-only Content-Security-Policy, except that images and fetches may also use blob: URLs, which only the page's own scripts make (textures inside 3D models), and X-Frame-Options: DENY; vendor static assets such as htmx and three.js locally instead of loading them from a CDN. (`web.security.headers`)
- Registration requires explicit consent to the terms of service and privacy policy, published at /terms and /privacy. (`web.signup.consent`)
- Opening a link that carries a token only renders a form; consume the token only on that form's POST, so email link scanners cannot spend it. (`web.tokens.post-only`)
- Brand files and episode media are stored by the AssetStore under SREDITOR_ASSETS_DIR (a Docker volume), named by content hash, and served only to channel members and only while the kit or an episode references them, with the security headers and a private immutable cache; images and episode media display inline, other files download. (`web.app.assets`)
- After a change, a signed-in page redirects (303, or HX-Redirect for htmx) so a reload does not repeat it, and the next page says what happened from a short-lived cookie that holds only a message key; a failed change re-renders the form with each error next to its field. (`web.app.feedback`)
- Put the signed-in pages in src/sreditor/web/workspace/, one module per area (channels, accounts, brand, editorial, episodes, library, members, account) with templates in templates/workspace/; they render server-side with Jinja2 and htmx like the public pages, call the service and store layer, and are left out of the OpenAPI schema. (`web.app.layout`)
- The signed-in area at /app lists the person's channels and offers, per channel, an overview with what it still needs, accounts, brand kit, editorial, episodes, the library of characters and locations, and members, plus settings for editors; /app/account holds the profile, password and API tokens. A new area adds one entry to the channel's menu. (`web.app.pages`)
- Signed-in pages need a session and send a visitor without one to sign in and back. A channel the person is not a member of answers 404, as the API does; actions their role does not allow are hidden, and their POST answers 403. (`web.app.permissions`)
- Forms show validation, rate-limit and expired-token errors next to the relevant field; the JSON endpoints stay unchanged for API clients. (`web.forms.errors`)
- Put the public pages in src/sreditor/web/: routes.py, Pydantic form models in forms.py, templates/ and static/; page routes call the store and service layer, never SQL. (`web.layout`)
- The public area offers /, /register, /register/sent, /verify, /login, /forgot-password, /reset-password, /invitations/{token}, /terms and /privacy; a signed-in visitor to / is redirected to the app. (`web.public.pages`)
